title: Expert hotstart: length skew & padding playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook of observations, microbenchmarks, and actionable mitigation ideas for a recurring production pattern: sudden per-request latency spikes in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models when serving long-context and length-skewed traffic (sometimes seen only after node restarts or autoscale events). The goal is to capture quick heuristics and experiment ideas for engineers on-call and runtime owners exploring root causes across Llama/Mistral/Qwen variants.

Background summary:
- Symptom: Intermittent p95/p99 token latency regressions (10–3x) after node warmup or bursty arrivals, disproportionately affecting long-context (>8k) requests and workloads with heavy length variance (short docs mixed with occasional very long queries).
- Affected models: observed on an MoE Llama-variant and a Mistral-MoE prototype; Qwen-base (non-MoE) used as baseline with fewer spikes but higher steady attention cost on long contexts.
- Environment: dedicated GPU pools (A100-equivalent), runtime uses continuous batching with per-model router and a shared KV cache. Quantized weights (4-bit) on some nodes.

High-level hypothesis (multi-factor):
1) Routing-induced serialization: when long requests trigger many expert-switches, router scheduling creates head-of-line stalls — small-population experts block pipeline progress because they require cross-stream synchronization and memory transfers.
2) Padding/length skew amplification: mixed-length batches increase wasted compute (padding) and cause KV cache thrashing when long requests push new cache addresses into hot set.
3) Cold expert state & IO: after scale-up or cold start, expert parameter pages / activation buffers are loaded lazily causing transient memcpy and cache-miss penalties.
4) Micro-batching heuristics unsuitable for long-context: default batch fragment size and routing window leave insufficient time to amortize router overhead for very long sequences.

Representative profiling snapshot (N = sample run on dev cluster):
- Workload: mixed-length generator: 70% short (<256 tokens), 25% medium (256–2048), 5% long (8k context + generation).
- Measured token-level breakdown (median of slow requests):
  - Router enqueue & gating: 22%
  - Attention compute (self-attn & cross-attn): 28%
  - KV IO (serialize/deserialize + copy): 18%
  - Expert kernel execution: 20%
  - Memcpy / device-host sync: 9%
  - Other (tokenization, postprocess): 3%
- Long-request cold p99 example: 1 token step p99 = 410 ms (baseline steady-state p99 = 120 ms)
- Trace snippets (annotated):
  - t=0ms: request accepted, router starts gating
  - t=45ms: expert selection completed, but expert memory fault triggers device memcpy
  - t=230ms: kernel execution runs but waits on cross-stream barrier for small expert batch
  - t=410ms: token emitted

Micro-experiments we ran (summaries):
A) Synthetic length-bucketed batching: enforce batches by request-length buckets (round-robin short/long disabled)
   - Result: p99 for long requests dropped ~35% vs mixed packing; overall throughput slightly reduced for short-only periods.
B) Router prefetch window increase (+30 ms): allow router to gather slightly more candidates before dispatch
   - Result: reduced head-of-line stalls in high-variance traces (~20% latency win), but increased median latency under saturated load.
C) Expert-state eager prefetch on scale-up: proactively touch expert pages after node join
   - Result: reduced cold-start memcpy spikes on first 50 requests; effect decays after TTL.
D) Short-request padding clamp: do not pad short requests beyond 64 tokens when co-batched with long-context items (pad-truncation)
   - Result: reduced compute waste; improved KV cache hit-rate marginally.
E) KV cache sticky TTL tuning: raise TTL for addresses hot within last 10k tokens
   - Result: fewer cache evictions under mixed workload; small memory overhead.

Key findings / interpretations:
- The router is a high-leverage component. Small increases to the dispatch window or minor batching adjustments materially reduce p99 under variance, but naive increases hurt median throughput. This indicates a tradeoff surface that should be surfaced as runtime knobs per-customer profile.
- Cold expert memory movement (memcpy) is a dominant contributor to first-request spikes after scaling events. Eager prefetching after allocation reduces tail latency with minimal steady cost — worth defaulting in Dedicated nodes.
- Padding is not just wasted FLOPs: when long and short are mixed, padding patterns drive KV cache churn and exacerbate serialization at the router. Packing by length buckets is a low-friction mitigation for customer workloads with identifiable length distributions.
- Non-MoE baselines (Qwen) avoid routing stalls but sustain a higher steady attention cost for long contexts — this makes them a viable fallback for extreme tail cases where MoE routing variance dominates.

Actionable playbook (quick runbook for on-call / infra owners):
- Immediate mitigations to try when p99 spikes observed:
  1) Toggle "eager-expert-prefetch" on recently scaled nodes (runtime flag) and monitor p99 for first 5 minutes.
  2) Enable length-bucket batching for the affected route (configurable at per-route policy) and observe p99/throughput tradeoffs.
  3) Temporarily increase router dispatch window by +20ms for routes serving >5% long-context requests.
- Medium-term changes to evaluate in A/B: 
  - Per-model routing profiles: allow different window/batch-fragment targets for MoE vs monolithic models.
  - Routing admission control: when expert-hotspots are detected, throttle or reroute some requests to compatible monolithic variants automatically.
  - Persistent expert warming: after node restart, schedule low-priority synthetic traffic to warm expert state without impacting production latency.
- Instrumentation to add (low-effort priorities):
  - Add per-expert cold-fault counters (increment on first-touch memcpy) + TTLed histogram for time-to-first-successful-kernel.
  - Emit per-request "length-skew-index": ratio of request length to batch mean length to correlate padding waste with latency.
  - Router backlog heatmap: per-epoch snapshot of candidates waiting vs dispatched to identify hotspot experts.

Open questions / experiments to prioritize:
1) Quantization interaction: does 4-bit quantization increase memcpy cost due to unpacking patterns for small experts? Run controlled kernels comparing 4-bit vs 8-bit expert kernels for memcpy+launch latency.
2) Cross-model routing policies: can a fast heuristic select monolithic fallbacks when expected router overhead exceeds a threshold derived from request length and expert-hit predictions?
3) Adaptive TTL: can we learn per-expert TTLs from traffic so hot experts survive bursts while cold ones are evicted aggressively?
4) Device-side scheduling: would moving some router logic into a lightweight CUDA kernel reduce host-device sync and improve overall headroom? Prototype dispatcher-on-device for small expert counts.

Notes / links for follow-ups:
- Related incidents: see INF-1892 for production timeline and heap profiles.
- PR with eager prefetch prototype: runtime/pull/2421 (benchmarks included in PR).
- Slack thread: #moe-runtime where Marina posted heatmaps (referenced in Confluence page).

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally:
1) Use the long-context repro harness: scripts/repro/length-skew-driver.py (select seed=17, mix ratio config)
2) Start runtime with --enable-eager-prefetch=false (toggle between runs)
3) Capture per-token traces (export TRACE=1) and run ./tools/trace-aggregator --group-by=expert-id
4) Compare KV hit-rate logs in /tmp/kvstats.json across runs

Concluding note:
This doc is intended as a compact troubleshooting and experiment guide rather than final recommendations. The interplay between routing, padding, and memory movement is complex and workload-dependent — our aim should be to expose conservative defaults that avoid the worst tails and to provide runtime knobs for power users.

[END OF PLAYBOOK]
